q: Which of the following is an autotroph? (JAC 2022)
e: A mango tree synthesises its own food by photosynthesis using chlorophyll, so it is an autotroph.

q: What is essential for autotrophic nutrition? (JAC 2021)
o: Carbon dioxide, water, chlorophyll and sunlight
e: Green plants require all four—CO₂, water, chlorophyll and sunlight—for photosynthesis.

q: With the help of which structure does Amoeba take in food? (JAC 2022)
e: Amoeba engulfs food using temporary finger-like extensions called pseudopodia to form a food vacuole.

q: Where does digestion of food occur in Amoeba? (JAC 2022)
e: Inside Amoeba's food vacuole, complex substances are broken down into simpler ones by digestive enzymes.

q: How many chambers are present in the human heart? (JAC 2022)
e: The human heart has four chambers: two upper atria (left and right) and two lower ventricles (left and right).

q: Which is the respiratory pigment in humans? (JAC 2022)
e: Haemoglobin in red blood corpuscles has a very high affinity for oxygen and carries O₂ throughout the body.

q: The kidneys in human beings are a part of the system for: (JAC 2021)
e: Kidneys filter nitrogenous wastes like urea from the blood to excrete urine, forming part of the excretory system.

q: What is the structural and functional unit of the kidney called? (JAC 2022)
e: Each kidney has large numbers of filtration units called nephrons packed close together.

q: The xylem in plants is responsible for: (JAC 2021, 2022)
e: Xylem tissue transports water and dissolved minerals absorbed from the soil upward to the plant body.

q: Transport of food (products of photosynthesis) in plants takes place through: (JAC 2022)
e: Phloem transports soluble products of photosynthesis (food) from leaves to other parts of the plant.

q: Which enzyme is present in saliva? (JAC 2022)
e: Saliva contains the enzyme salivary amylase that breaks down complex starch into simple sugars.

q: Absorption of digested food mainly takes place in which organ? (JAC 2022, 2025)
e: The small intestine is the site of complete digestion, and its inner lining has villi that absorb digested food.

q: Which blood cells help in clotting of blood? (JAC 2022)
e: Platelets circulate around the body and help clot the blood at points of injury to stop bleeding.

q: What is the main food product formed during photosynthesis? (JAC 2022)
e: Photosynthesis synthesises carbohydrates (glucose) from CO₂ and water, releasing oxygen as a by-product.

q: Exchange of gases in plants takes place mainly through which structures on leaves?
e: Stomata are tiny pores present on the surface of leaves through which massive amounts of gaseous exchange occur.

q: Where are alveoli found? (JAC 2025)
e: Within the lungs, air passages divide into smaller tubes terminating in balloon-like structures called alveoli.

q: Which acid is secreted in the human stomach?
e: Gastric glands secrete hydrochloric acid (HCl), which creates an acidic medium for pepsin and kills bacteria.

q: In which organ of the body is bile juice produced?
e: Bile juice is produced by the liver and temporarily stored in the gall bladder.

q: Which mode of nutrition is found in humans? (JAC 2022)
e: Humans (and Amoeba) ingest whole food and digest and absorb it inside their body, which is holozoic nutrition.

q: Which of the following is a parasitic plant?
e: Cuscuta lacks chlorophyll and derives nutrition from living host plants without killing them (parasitic nutrition).

q: What is the normal systolic and diastolic blood pressure in humans?
e: Normal systolic pressure is about 120 mm of Hg and diastolic pressure is about 80 mm of Hg.

q: Which instrument is used to measure blood pressure?
e: Blood pressure is measured with an instrument called a sphygmomanometer.

q: In anaerobic respiration, yeast converts pyruvate into:
e: During fermentation in yeast (absence of oxygen), pyruvate is converted into ethanol and carbon dioxide.

q: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach helps kill which harmful things entering with food?
e: Stomach HCl kills harmful microbes and bacteria that enter along with food.

q: The loss of water in the form of vapour from the aerial parts of a plant is known as: (JAC 2022)
e: The loss of water in the form of vapour from the aerial parts (mainly stomata) of a plant is called transpiration.

q: The procedure of removing nitrogenous wastes from blood using an artificial kidney is called: (JAC 2022)
e: When kidneys fail, removing nitrogenous wastes from the blood via an artificial kidney is called dialysis.

q: Which is the longest part of the human alimentary canal?
e: The small intestine is the longest part of the alimentary canal, fitted in a compact space by extensive coiling.

q: Which molecule is known as the energy currency of the cell?
e: Energy released in cellular respiration is used to synthesise ATP, which fuels cellular activities as the cell's energy currency.

q: How many chambers does a fish heart have?
e: Fishes have only two chambers in their heart (one atrium and one ventricle), showing single circulation.

q: The opening and closing of stomata is controlled by: (JAC 2026)
e: Guard cells swell when water flows into them causing the stomatal pore to open, and shrink when water leaves causing it to close.

q: In which part of the cell does the breakdown of glucose into pyruvate take place? (JAC 2022, 2024)
e: The breakdown of 6-carbon glucose into 3-carbon pyruvate occurs in the cytoplasm of all organisms.

q: The breakdown of pyruvate to give carbon dioxide, water and energy takes place in: (JAC 2022)
e: In the presence of oxygen, pyruvate breaks down completely into CO₂, water and energy inside mitochondria.

q: During vigorous exercise, due to lack of oxygen in muscle cells, pyruvate is converted into:
e: Lack of oxygen in muscle cells converts pyruvate into 3-carbon lactic acid, whose build-up causes cramps.

q: During photosynthesis, oxygen gas evolved comes from the splitting of: (JAC 2022)
e: During light reaction, photolysis splits water (H₂O) into hydrogen and oxygen, releasing O₂ gas.

q: Which of the following is NOT required for photosynthesis? (JAC 2022)
e: Carbohydrate is the product of photosynthesis, not a raw material. Required inputs are CO₂, water, chlorophyll and sunlight.

q: What is the function of pepsin enzyme in the stomach? (JAC 2022)
e: Pepsin secreted in the stomach digests proteins into simpler peptides in an acidic medium.

q: What protects the inner lining of the stomach from the action of acid under normal conditions? (JAC 2022)
e: Mucus secreted by gastric glands coats and protects the inner lining of the stomach from hydrochloric acid.

q: What are the two main functions of bile juice? (JAC 2022)
o: Digest starch and make food acidic
Make food alkaline and emulsify large fat globules into small ones
e: Bile makes acidic food alkaline for pancreatic enzymes and emulsifies large fat globules into tiny globules for lipase.

q: Lipase enzyme secreted by the pancreas digests: (JAC 2022)
e: Pancreatic juice contains trypsin for digesting proteins and lipase for breaking down emulsified fats.

q: Which of the following has the longest small intestine? (JAC 2022)
e: Herbivores like cows eat grass containing cellulose which takes longer to digest, so they have the longest small intestine.

q: What is one main function of lymph? (JAC 2020)
o: Carrying digested fat from intestine and draining excess extracellular fluid back into blood
e: Lymph carries digested and absorbed fat from the intestine and drains excess fluid from extracellular space back into blood.

q: Which blood vessel carries blood from the heart to various organs of the body? (JAC 2022)
e: Arteries are vessels that carry blood away from the heart to various organs; they have thick, elastic walls.

q: Why do arteries have thicker and more elastic walls than veins?
o: Because blood emerges from the heart under high pressure in them
Because they lie just beneath the skin
e: Blood flows from the heart into arteries under high pressure, requiring thick elastic walls to withstand it.

q: What is the purpose of valves present inside veins?
o: To ensure blood flows in only one direction and prevent backflow
e: Since blood in veins is no longer under high pressure, valves ensure unidirectional flow back toward the heart.

q: All arteries carry oxygenated blood EXCEPT:
e: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs for oxygenation.

q: In which of the following does transpiration play NO role? (JAC 2022)
o: Absorption and upward movement of minerals
e: Transpiration aids upward movement of water/minerals and cooling, whereas food transport is carried out by phloem.

q: According to the balanced equation of photosynthesis, how many molecules of CO₂ are needed to form 1 molecule of glucose?
e: Balanced equation: 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O. Thus 6 CO₂ molecules form 1 glucose molecule.

q: During the starch test of a leaf with iodine solution, the region containing starch turns:
e: Starch reacts with iodine solution to produce a characteristic blue-black colour.

q: Why is a potted plant kept in a dark room for 3 days before performing a photosynthesis experiment?
o: To destarch the leaves by using up previously stored starch
e: Keeping the plant in the dark uses up pre-existing starch reserves so any new starch formed clearly indicates photosynthesis during the test.

q: What prevents the air-passage (trachea) in the throat from collapsing when there is no air in it?
e: Rings of cartilage present in the throat/trachea ensure that the air passage does not collapse.

q: Which energy molecule is used in the active translocation of food in phloem?
e: Substances like sucrose are transferred into phloem tissue using energy from ATP, creating osmotic pressure that moves food.

q: How many heart chambers do amphibians and most reptiles have?
e: Amphibians and many reptiles have three-chambered hearts and can tolerate some mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.

q: What is the correct pathway of urine after it is formed in the kidneys?
e: Urine formed in each kidney passes through the ureter into the urinary bladder for storage and is released through the urethra.

q: Where and in what forms can plants store their waste products?
o: In cellular vacuoles and as resins and gums in old xylem
Only as crystals on leaf surface
e: Plants store wastes in cellular vacuoles, leaves that fall off, and as resins and gums especially in old xylem.

q: Which of the following is an example of saprotrophic nutrition?
e: Fungi like bread mould, yeast and mushrooms break down food material outside the body and then absorb it (saprotrophic).

q: Which three main substances are secreted by gastric glands in the stomach?
e: Gastric glands in the stomach wall release hydrochloric acid, the protein-digesting enzyme pepsin, and protective mucus.

q: What are the final digested products of proteins, carbohydrates and fats respectively in the small intestine?
o: Amino acids, glucose, fatty acids and glycerol
e: Intestinal enzymes finally convert proteins to amino acids, complex carbohydrates to glucose, and fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

q: What adaptation do desert plants show in photosynthesis to prevent water loss?
o: Keeping stomata wide open all day
Taking up CO₂ at night to form an intermediate acted upon by chlorophyll energy during the day
e: Desert plants take up CO₂ at night and prepare an intermediate which is acted upon by energy absorbed by chlorophyll during the day.

q: How does the lower amount of dissolved oxygen in water compared to air affect aquatic organisms?
o: Their breathing rate is slower than terrestrial organisms
Their breathing rate is much faster than that of terrestrial organisms
e: Because dissolved oxygen in water is fairly low compared to oxygen in air, aquatic organisms have a much faster rate of breathing.

q: What is the cup-shaped structure at the beginning of a nephron enclosing the glomerulus called?
e: Each nephron begins with a cup-shaped Bowman's capsule enclosing a cluster of thin-walled blood capillaries called the glomerulus.

q: In the bell-jar photosynthesis experiment, why is a watch-glass containing potassium hydroxide (KOH) placed beside one plant?
e: Potassium hydroxide absorbs carbon dioxide inside the bell jar, proving that CO₂ is essential for photosynthesis.

q: Which sequence correctly represents double circulation in humans?
o: Lungs → Right atrium → Right ventricle → Body
Body → Left atrium → Left ventricle → Lungs
Body → Right atrium → Right ventricle → Lungs → Left atrium → Left ventricle → Body
Lungs → Left ventricle → Right ventricle → Body
e: Deoxygenated blood goes Body → Right atrium → Right ventricle → Lungs, and oxygenated blood returns Lungs → Left atrium → Left ventricle → Body.

q: Why do ventricles have thicker muscular walls than atria?
o: Because ventricles have to pump blood into various organs under high pressure
Because atria do not receive blood
e: Atria only push blood into adjacent ventricles, whereas ventricles pump blood to the lungs and the entire body.

q: If a person's bile duct gets blocked, the digestion of which food component will be most affected?
e: Bile emulsifies large fat globules so pancreatic lipase can act efficiently; without bile, fat digestion is greatly impaired.

q: Which useful substances are selectively reabsorbed from the initial filtrate in a nephron?
o: Glucose, amino acids, salts and a major amount of water
e: As the filtrate flows along the nephron tubule, useful substances like glucose, amino acids, salts and water are selectively reabsorbed.

q: When air is blown from the mouth into lime water versus pumped with a pichkari, why does mouth-blown air turn lime water milky much faster?
o: Exhaled air contains a much higher percentage of CO₂ produced by respiration
Mouth air has no water vapour
e: Atmospheric air has only ~0.04% CO₂, whereas exhaled air has much higher CO₂ from cellular respiration, rapidly forming white CaCO₃ precipitate.

q: In a healthy adult, the initial filtrate in kidneys is about 180 L daily, yet the urine actually excreted is only 1–2 L. Why?
o: Most of the filtrate (water and useful solutes) is selectively reabsorbed in the nephron tubules
e: About 99% of the initial filtrate is reabsorbed back into the blood by the renal tubules.

q: How are the numerous villi on the inner lining of the small intestine beneficial?
o: They greatly increase the surface area for absorption and are richly supplied with blood vessels
e: Villi enormously increase surface area for absorption and contain rich blood capillaries to transport absorbed food to cells.

q: What will happen if a thick coat of Vaseline is applied to the lower surface of a plant's leaves?
o: Stomata will get blocked, halting gaseous exchange and transpiration
e: Most stomata lie on the lower leaf surface; Vaseline seals them, preventing gaseous exchange for respiration/photosynthesis and stopping transpiration.

q: If salivary amylase is lacking in saliva, which event in the mouth cavity will be affected?
e: Salivary amylase initiates the digestion of complex starch into simple sugars right inside the mouth.

q: What is the major difference in energy release between aerobic and anaerobic respiration?
o: Aerobic respiration releases vastly more energy (ATP) due to complete breakdown of glucose
e: Aerobic respiration completely oxidises glucose into CO₂ and H₂O, yielding far greater energy than anaerobic respiration.

q: What is the colourless fluid containing less protein that escapes from blood capillaries into intercellular spaces called?
e: Plasma, some proteins and blood cells escape through capillary pores into intercellular spaces to form tissue fluid or lymph.

q: Which is the major driving force in the movement of water in xylem during the day?
e: During the day when stomata are open, transpiration creates a suction pull that draws water upward from roots through xylem.

q: Where and by what process does exchange of gases occur in the human lungs? (JAC 2025)
e: Gaseous exchange between thin alveolar walls and surrounding blood capillaries occurs via diffusion down concentration gradients.

q: What regulates the exit of food from the stomach into the small intestine in small amounts?
e: The exit of food from the stomach into the small intestine is regulated by a sphincter muscle.

q: When guard cells become flaccid (shrink due to water loss), what happens to the stomatal pore?
e: When guard cells lose water and shrink, the stomatal pore closes to prevent excess water loss.

q: What will be the direct consequence if there is a severe deficiency of haemoglobin in human blood?
o: Tissues receive insufficient oxygen causing fatigue and lack of energy (anaemia)
e: Without adequate haemoglobin to transport oxygen from lungs to tissues, cellular respiration and energy production drop sharply.

q: Why are the left and right sides of the human heart completely separated by a septum?
o: To prevent mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood, ensuring high oxygen supply for high energy needs
So both sides carry impure blood
e: Warm-blooded animals (birds and mammals) constantly use energy to maintain body temperature, requiring efficient non-mixed oxygen delivery.

q: What is the rhythmic contraction of muscles along the alimentary canal that pushes food forward called?
e: The lining of the canal has muscles that contract rhythmically (peristaltic movements) to push the food forward in a regulated manner.

q: In a cross-section of a leaf, which cells contain green dots called chloroplasts?
o: Palisade/spongy mesophyll cells and guard cells
e: Chloroplasts containing chlorophyll are present in the mesophyll cells beneath the upper epidermis and in guard cells.

q: How do the ribs and diaphragm move when we breathe in (inhale)?
o: Ribs move down/inward and diaphragm arches up
Ribs lift up/outward and diaphragm flattens
Ribs stay still and diaphragm vanishes
e: During inhalation, we lift our ribs and flatten our diaphragm, increasing chest cavity volume so air rushes into the lungs.

q: How does the transport of CO₂ in human blood differ from that of oxygen?
o: CO₂ goes mainly by haemoglobin and O₂ dissolved in plasma
O₂ is carried mainly by haemoglobin in RBCs, whereas CO₂ being more soluble in water is mostly transported in dissolved form in blood
e: Carbon dioxide is more soluble in water than oxygen is, hence CO₂ is mostly transported in the dissolved form in our blood.

q: In the absence of stomach acid (HCl), which enzyme in the stomach would fail to get activated properly?
e: Pepsin requires an acidic medium created by HCl in order to act efficiently on proteins.

q: How does the direction of transport in phloem differ from that in xylem?
o: Xylem transport is unidirectional (upward) while phloem translocation occurs in both upward and downward directions
Phloem is upward only and xylem is bidirectional
e: Water moves only upward in xylem, whereas phloem translocates food both upward and downward depending on the plant's needs.

q: Which gas produced by yeast during fermentation makes bread dough rise and become spongy?
e: Anaerobic respiration in yeast releases carbon dioxide gas along with ethanol, making dough rise.

q: If the Bowman's capsule of nephrons is damaged, which process is immediately affected?
e: The glomerulus and Bowman's capsule together perform filtration of blood to form the initial glomerular filtrate.

q: Both Amoeba and Paramoecium are unicellular, yet how does food intake in Paramoecium differ from Amoeba?
o: Paramoecium has a definite shape and food is taken in at a specific spot moved there by cilia
e: Unlike Amoeba which engulfs food anywhere via pseudopodia, Paramoecium has a definite shape and uses cilia covering its surface to sweep food to a specific spot.

q: Why is diffusion insufficient to meet the oxygen requirements of multicellular organisms like humans?
o: Because not all cells are in direct contact with the surrounding environment and diffusion is far too slow
e: In large multicellular organisms, interior cells are not in direct contact with the environment and simple diffusion is far too slow to reach deep cells.

q: Why do lungs always contain a residual volume of air even after forceful exhalation?
o: So that there is sufficient time for oxygen to be absorbed and carbon dioxide to be released
e: Residual air ensures continuous availability of air so there is sufficient time for oxygen absorption and CO₂ release between breaths.

q: Which force plays a major role in pushing water upward in xylem at night when stomata are closed?
e: At night when transpiration is minimal, root pressure generated by active ion uptake pushes water upward in xylem.

q:
Assertion (A): Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is secreted in the human stomach.
Reason (R): HCl creates an acidic medium which facilitates the action of the enzyme pepsin and kills bacteria.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains why HCl is secreted in the stomach.

q:
Assertion (A): Herbivores like cows have a longer small intestine than carnivores like lions.
Reason (R): Cellulose present in grass takes a longer time to digest.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation: digesting cellulose requires a longer tract than meat.

q:
Assertion (A): The right and left sides of the human heart are separated by a septum.
Reason (R): This prevents mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood, ensuring efficient oxygen supply for high energy needs.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains why complete separation of the two sides is essential.

q:
Assertion (A): Water transport in plant xylem happens solely by active ATP consumption by living cells.
Reason (R): Evaporation of water from stomata creates a suction pull (transpiration pull) that draws water upwards.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: A is false because xylem vessels are non-living tubes driven physically by root pressure and transpiration pull; R is true.

q:
Assertion (A): Arteries possess valves to prevent backflow of blood.
Reason (R): Arteries have thick and elastic walls.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: A is false because valves are present in veins (not arteries, where blood flows under high pressure). R is true.

q:
Assertion (A): Desert plants keep their stomata closed during the day yet perform photosynthesis.
Reason (R): They take up CO₂ at night to form an intermediate acted upon by energy absorbed by chlorophyll during the day.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R is the exact explanation of how desert plants photosynthesise without losing excess water.

q:
Assertion (A): Muscle cramps often occur after sudden vigorous running.
Reason (R): In lack of oxygen, pyruvate is converted into lactic acid in muscle cells.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains the cause of muscle cramps.

q:
Assertion (A): Nutrition in Amoeba is holozoic.
Reason (R): Amoeba breaks down food outside its body like saprotrophs and then absorbs it.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: A is true (Amoeba ingests food and digests it inside a food vacuole), while R is false (extracellular digestion is saprotrophic).

q:
Assertion (A): Translocation of food by phloem is an active process requiring ATP.
Reason (R): Transfer of sucrose into phloem using ATP increases osmotic pressure, causing water to enter and move material to tissues with less pressure.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R accurately explains the mechanism of phloem translocation.

q:
Assertion (A): Aquatic animals have a slower breathing rate than terrestrial animals.
Reason (R): The amount of dissolved oxygen in water is fairly low compared to the amount of oxygen in air.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: A is false because aquatic organisms breathe much faster due to low dissolved O₂ in water; R is true.

q:
Assertion (A): In haemodialysis, the patient's blood is passed through semi-permeable tubes.
Reason (R): The dialysing fluid has the same osmotic pressure as blood except it lacks nitrogenous wastes, so wastes diffuse out of the blood.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R explains how nitrogenous wastes are removed by diffusion during dialysis.

q:
Assertion (A): Villi in the small intestine are richly supplied with blood vessels.
Reason (R): Absorbed food needs to be quickly transported to each and every cell of the body.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

q:
Assertion (A): Fishes show single circulation.
Reason (R): Blood passes through the fish heart twice during each cycle.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: A is true, while R is false because blood goes through the fish heart only once in each cycle.

q:
Assertion (A): Food coming from the stomach is alkaline and bile juice makes it acidic.
Reason (R): Pancreatic enzymes act in an alkaline medium.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: A is false (food from the stomach is acidic and bile makes it alkaline). R is true.

q:
Assertion (A): Conversion of pyruvate to ethanol and CO₂ occurs anaerobically in yeast.
Reason (R): This reaction takes place inside mitochondria in the presence of oxygen.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: A is true, while R is false because fermentation in yeast takes place in the absence of oxygen.

q: Case Study: Two healthy potted plants X and Y were destarched in the dark for 3 days, then placed under separate bell jars. A watch-glass with KOH was placed inside jar X, and nothing inside jar Y. After 2 hours in sunlight, leaves from both were tested for starch. What is observed?
o: Leaf from plant X does not turn blue-black, whereas leaf from plant Y turns blue-black
Leaf from Y does not turn blue-black, while X does
e: KOH absorbed CO₂ in jar X so no photosynthesis or starch occurred there, whereas plant Y had CO₂ and tested positive (blue-black) for starch.

q: Case Study (based on the same setup): Why are the bottoms of both bell jars sealed to the glass plate using Vaseline?
o: To keep the setup air-tight so outside atmospheric CO₂ cannot enter
e: If not sealed air-tight with Vaseline, outside air containing CO₂ would enter jar X and invalidate the control.

q: Case Study: A variegated leaf (with green and white patches) was destarched, exposed to sunlight for 6 hours, boiled in alcohol, and dipped in iodine. Only the previously green patches turned blue-black. What does this prove?
e: Starch formed only in green regions containing chlorophyll, proving chlorophyll is necessary for photosynthesis.

q: Case Study (same experiment): Why is the leaf boiled in alcohol using a water bath before testing with iodine?
o: To add glucose to the leaf
To decolourise the leaf by removing chlorophyll so the blue-black stain is clearly visible (water bath avoids catching fire)
e: Boiling in alcohol removes green chlorophyll that masks the blue-black iodine colour; a water bath prevents flammable alcohol from igniting.

q: Case Study: A student took 1 mL starch solution in two test tubes A and B. She added 1 mL saliva only to tube A. After 30 minutes, iodine was added to both. Tube A showed no blue-black colour while tube B turned blue-black. Why?
o: Salivary amylase in tube A broke down starch into simple sugars
e: Salivary amylase digested starch in tube A into sugars, so it gave a negative iodine test unlike undigested starch in tube B.

q: Case Study: A patient with double kidney failure undergoes dialysis thrice a week. Compared to a healthy natural kidney, which crucial step does NOT occur in an artificial kidney (dialysis unit)?
e: Unlike natural nephrons, an artificial kidney removes wastes by diffusion without any selective reabsorption mechanism.

q: Case Study: A patient has a leaky valve near the left ventricle. Normally, when the left ventricle contracts, where is blood pumped directly?
o: Via aorta to the rest of the body
e: Oxygenated blood from the left atrium enters the left ventricle, which contracts to pump it through the aorta to the whole body.

q:
Assertion (A): A severe drop in blood platelets can cause prolonged bleeding even from minor wounds.
Reason (R): Platelets help clot blood at the site of injury to plug leaks.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R accurately explains why platelet deficiency leads to prolonged bleeding.

q:
Assertion (A): Food transport in tall trees happens only downward due to gravity.
Reason (R): Translocation in phloem takes place in both upward and downward directions according to the plant's needs.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: A is false because phloem transports stored sugar upward in spring to growing buds as well as downward to roots; R is true.

q: Case Study: After a 400 m sprint, an athlete's breathing rate and heart rate both increased sharply. Why does the body increase both together?
o: To supply more O₂ to muscles for higher ATP demand and rapidly remove extra CO₂
e: Faster breathing boosts O₂ intake and CO₂ removal, while faster heart pumping delivers oxygenated blood rapidly to working muscles.

q:
Assertion (A): Nitrogenous wastes like urea and uric acid are removed by the lungs.
Reason (R): Carbon dioxide is separated from blood in the lungs, whereas nitrogenous wastes are filtered from blood in the kidneys.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: A is false because nitrogenous wastes are filtered by kidneys, not lungs; R is true.

q: Case Study: A student carefully removed a ring of bark (containing phloem) around a plant stem while keeping the inner xylem intact. What is most likely observed after a few weeks?
o: Leaves wilt immediately as water stops rising
Leaves stay green temporarily via intact xylem, while the stem swells above the ring due to accumulated food and roots starve
e: The girdling experiment confirms xylem carries water upward while phloem carries food downward—food accumulates above the removed bark ring.

q:
Assertion (A): Nitrogen is an essential element used in the synthesis of proteins and other compounds in plants.
Reason (R): Plants directly absorb atmospheric N₂ gas through leaf stomata to make proteins.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: A is true, while R is false because plants take up nitrogen from soil as inorganic nitrates/nitrites or organic compounds fixed by bacteria.

q:
Assertion (A): A plant can get rid of stored waste products by shedding its old leaves.
Reason (R): Plants possess specialised excretory organs just like animals.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: A is true, while R is false because plants do not have specialised animal-like excretory organs.

q: Case Study: Four digestive secretions are paired with their target substrate and site of action. Which pairing is 100% correct?
o: Salivary amylase — Large intestine — Protein digestion
e: Trypsin secreted by the pancreas acts on proteins in the alkaline environment of the small intestine.

q: If a green plant is illuminated continuously only with monochromatic green light for 24 hours, how will the rate of photosynthesis be affected?
o: It will be maximum since leaves are green
It will drop drastically because chlorophyll reflects green light rather than absorbing it well
It will double compared to blue light
Stomata will release O₂ without photosynthesis
e: Green leaves reflect green wavelengths and absorb red and blue wavelengths strongly; hence photosynthesis is minimal under pure green light.

q: What is the key structural similarity between alveoli in the lungs and nephrons/glomeruli in the kidneys?
o: Both have only arteries, no capillaries
Both possess an extensive network of extremely thin-walled capillaries providing a huge surface area for exchange or filtration
e: Both rely on massive surface area and ultra-thin capillary networks—alveoli for gas diffusion and glomeruli/tubules for filtration and reabsorption.

q: Among Renal Artery, Renal Vein, and Hepatic Vein, which contains blood with the LOWEST concentration of urea?
e: The kidney filters urea out of blood entering via the renal artery, so blood leaving via the renal vein has the lowest urea concentration.

q: If the pH inside the small intestine drops to 2.5 despite healthy liver and pancreas, which group of enzymes will fail to work properly?
e: Trypsin and pancreatic lipase require an alkaline pH in the small intestine; an acidic pH of 2.5 inhibits their activity.

q: What is the number of carbon atoms in the carbon-compound product formed in (P) yeast fermentation, (Q) oxygen-starved muscle cells, and (R) aerobic breakdown in mitochondria respectively?
e: Yeast forms ethanol (2-carbon), hypoxic muscle forms lactic acid (3-carbon), and mitochondria release CO₂ (1-carbon). Sequence: 2, 3, 1.

q: If a Hydrilla plant is kept in water in sunlight and a small amount of sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃) is added to the water, what happens to the rate of oxygen bubble evolution?
o: Rate increases because NaHCO₃ increases dissolved CO₂ availability
e: Sodium bicarbonate supplies extra dissolved CO₂ in water, boosting the rate of photosynthesis and O₂ bubble evolution.

q: A newborn has a hole in the septum separating the left and right ventricles. What is the most direct physiological consequence?
o: Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix partially, lowering oxygen delivery to tissues
e: A ventricular septal hole allows oxygenated and deoxygenated blood to mix, reducing the efficiency of oxygen supply to body tissues.

q: Which of the following four statements regarding transport in plants is INCORRECT?
o: Xylem transport relies mainly on physical forces (root pressure and transpiration pull)
Phloem transports only amino acids and not sucrose
Xylem forms a continuous network of vessels and tracheids across roots, stems and leaves
e: Phloem transports soluble products of photosynthesis (mainly sucrose) in addition to amino acids and other substances; thus statement C is false.

q: Under which condition will a healthy green terrestrial plant close its stomata even during bright daytime?
o: When soil has plenty of water
When water loss exceeds water uptake causing severe water stress in the plant
e: During water stress, guard cells lose turgidity and shrink, closing stomata to prevent lethal dehydration.

q: Among the four parts of the alimentary canal—(1) Mouth cavity, (2) Stomach, (3) Small intestine, (4) Large intestine—in which parts does enzymatic chemical digestion occur?
e: Chemical digestion occurs in the mouth (starch), stomach (protein) and small intestine (all nutrients); the large intestine mainly absorbs remaining water.

q: A student claims that 100% of CO₂ in human blood is carried by haemoglobin, and 0% in plasma. Which experimental observation refutes this claim?
o: CO₂ is much more soluble in water than O₂, so it is mostly transported in dissolved form in blood plasma
e: NCERT explicitly states that carbon dioxide is more soluble in water than oxygen and hence is mostly transported in the dissolved form in our blood.

q: In a sealed sunlit aquarium containing both green aquatic plants and fishes, how do dissolved O₂ and CO₂ levels change between midday and midnight?
o: Midday has max CO₂ and min O₂
During the day photosynthesis outpaces respiration so O₂ rises and CO₂ drops; at night only respiration occurs so CO₂ rises and O₂ falls
O₂ keeps rising day and night
Fishes stop releasing CO₂ at night
e: By day photosynthesis exceeds respiration (net O₂ release, CO₂ uptake); at night only respiration occurs in both plants and fish (net CO₂ release, O₂ consumption).

q: Which order correctly arranges blood vessels from HIGHEST to LOWEST average blood pressure?
e: Blood leaves the left ventricle under maximum pressure in the aorta, drops across capillaries, and reaches its lowest pressure in the vena cava.

q: Even though glucose is normally 100% reabsorbed in nephron tubules, under what condition does glucose appear in urine?
o: When blood glucose rises so high (as in diabetes) that it exceeds the tubules' reabsorption limit
e: When blood sugar is abnormally elevated (diabetes), the nephron's reabsorption capacity is exceeded and glucose spills into urine.

q: In Class 10 Biology, which pair correctly distinguishes 'pseudopodia' from 'villi'?
o: Pseudopodia in intestine and villi in Amoeba
Pseudopodia are temporary extensions in Amoeba for engulfing food, whereas villi are permanent finger-like projections in the small intestine for absorption
e: Pseudopodia are temporary extensions of Amoeba's cell surface for ingestion, while villi are permanent finger-like folds lining the small intestine for absorption.

q: Why does phloem translocation slow down significantly if a plant's root/stem cells are deprived of oxygen?
o: Because lack of oxygen lowers ATP production by respiration, and phloem translocation uses ATP energy
e: Active loading of sucrose into phloem requires ATP produced mainly by aerobic respiration, so oxygen deprivation slows translocation.

q: If the opening between the left atrium and left ventricle gets partially blocked, where will back-pressure of blood build up first?
o: In the lungs and pulmonary veins
From right ventricle straight to small intestine
e: The left atrium receives blood directly from the lungs via pulmonary veins, so obstruction after it creates immediate back-pressure into the lungs.

q: What evolutionary advantage caused birds and mammals to develop a 4-chambered heart unlike amphibians?
o: Maximum unmixed oxygen supply for continuous high energy production to maintain constant body temperature
e: Birds and mammals require high energy continuously to maintain constant body temperature regardless of environment, necessitating 4-chambered separation.

q: Both respiration and combustion oxidise organic fuel into CO₂, H₂O and energy. How is cellular respiration fundamentally different from combustion?
o: Cellular respiration occurs slowly at body temperature in enzyme-controlled steps, trapping energy as ATP without flames
e: Respiration proceeds gradually via enzyme-catalysed steps at body temperature and conserves energy in ATP molecules, unlike sudden flame combustion.

q: Under which condition does a green leaf carry out respiration without releasing net O₂ into the air?
o: Bright noon sunlight with plenty of water
e: At night, absence of sunlight stops photosynthesis while respiration continues, resulting in net CO₂ release and no O₂ evolution.

q: If a patient's gall bladder is surgically removed, what happens to bile production and fat digestion?
o: The liver still produces bile reaching the intestine directly, though digesting very heavy fatty meals at once becomes harder due to no concentrated bile storage
e: Bile is made by the liver and only stored in the gall bladder. Without the gall bladder, bile still enters the intestine directly, though large fatty meals are harder to emulsify quickly.

q: A green leaf is placed in each of two closed bottles with a CO₂-sensitive indicator (turns yellow in high CO₂, purple in low CO₂). Bottle 1 is kept in bright sunlight and Bottle 2 is wrapped in black paper. What results after 2 hours?
o: Bottle 1 turns purple (low CO₂) and Bottle 2 turns yellow (high CO₂)
Bottle 1 turns yellow and Bottle 2 turns purple
e: In sunlight (Bottle 1), photosynthesis consumes CO₂ (low CO₂ → purple); in darkness (Bottle 2), respiration accumulates CO₂ (high CO₂ → yellow).

q: What are the smallest one-cell-thick blood vessels called, and why is their wall only one-cell thick?
o: Capillaries — to enable efficient exchange of materials between blood and surrounding cells across thin walls
e: Capillaries have walls that are only one cell thick so nutrients, gases and wastes exchange easily across them between blood and tissue cells.

q: The rhythmic volume change of the human thoracic cavity during breathing is caused by coordinated action of which two structures?
e: Intercostal muscles lift the ribs outward/upward while the diaphragm contracts and flattens, expanding chest volume for inhalation.

q: Arrange the following steps of urine formation and excretion in the correct sequence: (1) Collecting duct, (2) Filtration in glomerulus & Bowman's capsule, (3) Selective reabsorption along tubule, (4) Ureter
e: First glomerular filtration (2), then selective reabsorption along the tubule (3), entry into collecting duct (1), and transport through ureter (4).

q: Which metabolic waste product generated during photosynthesis in plants is vital for the survival of aerobic organisms?
e: As noted in NCERT Excretion in Plants, oxygen generated during photosynthesis can be thought of as a waste product of that process.

q: Why does carbon monoxide (CO) inhalation become fatal in a poorly ventilated room?
o: CO binds to haemoglobin far more strongly than O₂, blocking oxygen transport to body tissues
e: Carbon monoxide has much higher affinity for haemoglobin than oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and starving cells of oxygen.

q: In which vertebrate group does the heart always pump ONLY deoxygenated blood?
e: A fish heart receives deoxygenated blood from the body and pumps it to gills, from where oxygenated blood goes straight to the body without returning to the heart.

q: Efficient digestion of fats in the small intestine requires coordinated secretions from which two digestive glands?
o: Liver (bile for emulsification) and Pancreas (lipase for breakdown)
e: First bile from the liver emulsifies large fat globules into small droplets, increasing surface area for pancreatic lipase to digest them.

q: Which option accurately distinguishes blood from lymph?
o: Lymph has more RBCs and proteins
Blood is red (has RBCs/haemoglobin) pumped through heart, whereas lymph is colourless (lacks RBCs, less protein) and flows unidirectionally from tissues back into blood
Both are red and have haemoglobin
e: Blood contains RBCs/haemoglobin and higher proteins, whereas lymph is colourless, lacks RBCs, has less protein, and drains from intercellular spaces back into large veins.
